name: Agent Database Access and Permissions
title: Agent Database Access and Permissions
answer: When an AI agent queries a database on behalf of a user, it should see only what that user may see. Row level security, scoped credentials, read only roles and audit logging are the controls that keep an agent from becoming a way around existing permissions. The scope covers the whole path from the agent's tool call to the SQL that reaches the database, including the identity the connection carries. It also covers what the agent is allowed to do, not just what it can read.

sections.body: When an AI agent queries a database on behalf of a user, it should see only what that user may see. Row level security, scoped credentials, read only roles and audit logging are the controls that keep an agent from becoming a way around existing permissions. The scope covers the whole path from the agent's tool call to the SQL that reaches the database, including the identity the connection carries. It also covers what the agent is allowed to do, not just what it can read.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The agent usually reaches the database through a tool layer, often a Model Context Protocol server, which holds the connection and exposes a small set of query functions. This site tracks 2504 active MCP servers, 263 of them for SQL databases and warehouses, so that tool layer is a real and growing surface. Underneath, the controls live in the database itself: roles, grants, row level security policies, views, and connection pooling that can carry a per user identity. Audit logs may sit in the database, in the tool layer, or in a separate store.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common pattern is to give the agent a credential that maps to the requesting user, either by passing a token through to the database or by having the tool layer assume a role. Read only roles and restricted schemas limit what a mistaken or manipulated query can reach, and row level security policies filter rows by the user's attributes. Query rewriting, allow lists of tables and columns, and statement timeouts keep generated SQL inside bounds. Audit logging records the prompt, the SQL, the identity and the rows returned.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risk is privilege escalation by proxy, where an agent with broad credentials returns data the user could not fetch directly. Provenance matters because a generated query can be hard to attribute, so logs should tie each statement to a user, a session and a tool call. Access reviews, least privilege, and separation between the agent's service account and the user identity are common controls. Data access duties from regulation and contract still apply, and the agent does not change who is entitled to what.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more databases to expose native agent facing interfaces and finer grained policy that travels with the user identity. The 263 MCP servers for SQL databases and warehouses tracked here suggest the tool layer will keep expanding, and with it the need for standard ways to pass identity and scope. Work on policy as code, query attestation and per row audit is likely to mature. The direction is toward treating the agent as another client of the same permission system, not a special case.
